title: CAN A CHRISTIAN HUSBAND BE “INTOXICATED” WITH HIS WIFE’S LOVE?
paragraphs: CAN A CHRISTIAN HUSBAND BE “INTOXICATED” WITH HIS WIFE’S LOVE?
Proverbs Literally Uses That Kind of Language—and What God Says Next Could Rescue a Marriage Before Another Heart Gets Broken
There is a sentence in the Bible that sounds almost too passionate to be sitting in Proverbs.
Not borrowed from a romance novel.
Not invented by modern relationship culture.

And it tells a husband, in language startlingly intimate and unapologetically passionate, to become so captivated by the love of his own wife that some English translations reach for words such as “ravished,” “exhilarated,” “captivated,” or “infatuated” to communicate the Hebrew.
God is not embarrassed by marital desire.
And somewhere there may be a husband who desperately needs to hear that.
Because maybe you still love your wife...
but somewhere between bills, children, exhaustion, disagreements, disappointments, ministry, work, phones, responsibilities, aging bodies, unresolved wounds, and ordinary Tuesday nights...
You became roommates who remember being lovers.
You became business partners managing a household.
But somewhere along the road, something disappeared.
And the woman you once could barely stop thinking about became someone you sometimes barely notice.
Then Proverbs 5 walks into that quiet distance and says something astonishing.
“Let thy fountain be blessed: and rejoice with the wife of thy youth.”
“...let her breasts satisfy thee at all times; and be thou ravished always with her love.”
That is the language of the King James Version.
Yəhi məqorkha barukh, usəmaḥ me’eshet nə‘urekha.
“Let your fountain be blessed, and rejoice in the wife of your youth.”
אַיֶּ֥לֶת אֲהָבִ֗ים וְֽיַעֲלַת־חֵ֥ן דַּ֭דֶּיהָ יְרַוֻּ֣ךָ בְכָל־עֵ֑ת בְּ֝אַהֲבָתָ֗הּ תִּשְׁגֶּ֥ה תָמִֽיד׃
And that final phrase deserves our attention:
תִּשְׁגֶּה — tishgeh — comes from the Hebrew root שׁגה (shagah).

It can carry the sense of wandering, reeling, being led away, or being deeply carried along. That is one reason faithful English translations differ in how they express the force of the poetry. The KJV says “ravished.” Other translations use ideas such as being captivated, exhilarated, lost in love, or infatuated.
The Hebrew text unquestionably uses unusually intense language.
But here is what makes it even more powerful.
The same verb appears immediately afterward.
Proverbs 5:20 asks why the son should tishgeh with another woman.
Don't become intoxicated with what does not belong to you.
Become captivated again by the covenant love God has already placed beside you.
Biblical faithfulness is not merely refusing another woman's bed.
It is learning again to treasure your own wife.
It is possible for a man to be physically faithful while becoming emotionally absent.
But his eyes stopped lingering on his wife with affection.
His words stopped making her feel treasured.
And sometimes another kind of betrayal begins long before two bodies ever touch.
When pornography teaches a man to consume bodies instead of cherishing a person.
When a husband begins giving strangers the emotional energy his wife has been begging to receive.
Proverbs 5 refuses to reduce marital holiness to merely staying out of somebody else's bedroom.
God calls husbands toward something beautiful:
Christianity does not teach that marital sexuality is dirty and reluctantly tolerated by God.
God invented marriage before pornography corrupted desire.
God created the human body before lust distorted it.
God created marital intimacy before entertainment industries commercialized sexuality.
Sin takes God's gifts and tears them away from God's purposes.
And Proverbs 5 does something our culture desperately needs: it places passionate sexuality inside covenant faithfulness.
And there is something especially tender about the phrase “the wife of your youth.”
The body you married at twenty-five will not look identical at fifty-five.
That may be one of the most beautiful things an aging Christian marriage can preach without ever standing behind a pulpit.
“I knew you when we were young...
and I am still choosing you now.”
Imagine your wife knowing that she does not have to compete with edited bodies on a screen.
Imagine your husband knowing affection has not been replaced entirely by criticism.
Imagine children growing up watching two imperfect parents repent, forgive, laugh, touch, pray, disagree, reconcile, and keep choosing one another.
That does not mean pretending marriage is always romantic.
Sometimes resentment has accumulated for years.

Sometimes sexual intimacy is complicated by trauma, illness, childbirth, medication, disability, emotional wounds, exhaustion, betrayal, or seasons where professional and pastoral help may be necessary.
Proverbs 5 must never be weaponized to pressure a spouse sexually.
Love does not demand that another person's body become an instrument for selfish gratification.
That is where Jesus changes everything.
Because eventually every Christian marriage discovers an uncomfortable truth:
Two people enter marriage carrying expectations, insecurities, histories, temptations, wounds, selfishness, and blind spots.
And this is where a merely romantic vision of marriage collapses.
Because romance alone cannot carry the weight of two sinners for a lifetime.
The Gospel does not tell husbands, “Try harder to become perfect men so God will finally love you.”
The Gospel announces something infinitely greater.
He lived the righteousness we could not live.
He bore sin at the Cross.
And everyone who turns from sin and trusts in Him receives forgiveness and new life.
That Gospel changes the way a husband comes home.
Because a man who understands grace can finally say:
A wife transformed by grace can also repent when she has sinned.
Neither spouse becomes the savior of the marriage.
And suddenly marriage becomes something deeper than two people desperately demanding that the other person complete them.
It becomes two forgiven sinners learning how to give away the grace they themselves continually need.
Maybe that is what somebody reading this needs tonight.
Not another fantasy about somebody else's spouse.
Not another silent week sleeping beside someone whose heart you no longer know.
Maybe you need to turn around.
Look at the person God entrusted to you.
Because covenant is worth fighting for.
when was the last time you looked at your wife without looking through her?
When was the last time you told her something beautiful that had nothing to do with what she accomplished for you?
When was the last time you asked what was happening inside her heart and actually stayed quiet long enough to hear the answer?
When was the last time you held her without immediately asking for anything?
When was the last time you prayed over her?
When was the last time you thanked God for her?
when was the last time your husband knew that you still saw the man inside the responsibilities?
Marriage can become so familiar that we stop being amazed by the person standing beside us.
And notice what comes after Proverbs 5:19.
The chapter does not end with romance.
It returns to accountability before God.
“For the ways of man are before the eyes of the LORD...”
The husband scrolling secretly at midnight is seen.
The lonely wife crying quietly is seen.
The husband starving for affection is seen.
The repentance nobody else knows about is seen.
The couple trying desperately to rebuild is seen.
The person who closed the pornography page and cried out to Jesus is seen.
The husband who confessed what he had hidden is seen.
The wife who chose forgiveness while still establishing wise boundaries is seen.
And that truth is terrifying when we want darkness.
But breathtaking when we want restoration.
Because the God who exposes sin is also the God who sent His Son to save sinners.
Maybe your marriage has become a scandal.
Words you wish you could pull back into your mouth.
“You don't understand what happened in our house.”
And grace does not mean pretending the wound never happened.
Forgiveness does not make evil good.
Reconciliation does not eliminate the need for truth, repentance, safety, wisdom, accountability, or consequences.
But the Gospel means your worst chapter does not have to become the title of your entire story.
The Cross itself looked like history's darkest defeat.
He walks into graves and starts rewriting endings.
So maybe the first step tonight is not dramatic.
“I want Jesus to rebuild what I helped damage.”
Say them anyway when they are true.
Grace brings sinners into the light.
And if this article exposed something you have been hiding, don't turn conviction into shame and run from Christ.
Not because typing three words magically changes anything.
But because sometimes honesty begins when someone finally stops pretending.
Someone reading beneath you may realize they are not the only one.
Somebody desperately needs evidence that repentance is still possible, forgiveness is still real, and God is still working in ordinary homes.
There is no shame in needing prayer.
Not because every sentence will apply to every marriage, but because there may come a night when resentment whispers louder than covenant and you need to remember what Scripture actually said:
Be captivated continually by her love.
Send it privately to the brother drifting toward temptation before temptation becomes destruction.
Share it with the couple trying to rebuild.
And yes, share it with the single believer too, because the time to develop a biblical theology of marriage is not after temptation arrives.
If Gospel Warrior has been feeding your faith, stay close.

do not leave this article merely thinking about Gospel Warrior.
Think about the person sleeping beside you.
Think about what has quietly stolen your attention.
Then remember the strange, beautiful, startling command buried inside Proverbs:
Rejoice in the wife of your youth.
Because the world will continuously offer counterfeit intoxications.
Something that promises pleasure without covenant and eventually demands a price it never mentioned at the beginning.
Back to the woman you promised to love.
Back to the husband you promised to honor.
Maybe the miracle your marriage needs does not begin when your spouse finally becomes everything you wanted.
Maybe it begins when Jesus becomes Lord again over the parts of your heart you quietly took back from Him.
Because sometimes the most dangerous affair begins long before another person enters the room.
It begins when your heart leaves home.
And sometimes restoration begins with something equally quiet:
The world says the thrill is somewhere else. Wisdom whispers: look again at the covenant God placed beside you—and let Christ teach your wandering heart how to come home.
